newsitem.title: DENMARK: Minister says optimism due for Danish economy.
newsitem.headline: Minister says optimism due for Danish economy.

text.p: Danish economy minister Marianne Jelved said on Tuesday that the latest ministerial forecast gave cause for optimism about the state of the economy, but called for restraint in upcoming wage negotiations.
"The good development in the Danish economy gives cause for optimism, but if we are to continue to make advance, we must not squander these good results," Jelved said in a statement.

The Danish economy ministry released on Tuesday its latest economic survey, raising the GDP (gross domestic product) growth forecast for 1996 to 2.2 percent from 2.0 percent forecasted in October. It lowered 1997 GDP growth forecast to 2.9 percent from 3.1 percent.

Among other key data, it left its October inflation forecasts of 2.1 percent inflation in 1996, rising to 2.3 percent in 1997 unchanged, foreseeing the public sector budget deficit going into 2.0 billion crown surplus in 1997 and 4.8 billion crowns in 1998 after an expected 16.7 billion crown shortfall this year.
"The Danish economy is in much better balance than for many years. Unemployment continues to fall and there is a stable current account surplus," Jelved said.
Jelved said though that the next challenge would be spring 1997's two-year collective wage bargaining negotiations and appealed for pay restraint.
"Pay in Denmark is rising at a somewhat higher level than in our most important trading partners. This could put the current account surplus and employment at risk," she said.
"The government calls upon the employers and unions to negotiate pay deals which will ensure that the number of jobless can go on falling," she said.
Jelved said that the Danish government intended to continue its policies of moderate fiscal tightening in 1998, stressing the need to bring down Denmark's foreign debt.
"Denmark's foreign debt is still far too big and so it is necessary that we can go on posting solid current account surpluses," she said.

Denmark's foreign debt stands at around 250 billion crowns and the Central Bank estimates that it will take a decade to repay provided the present current account surplus remains the same at around four percent of GDP before interest payments.
The ministry's forecast saw the current account surplus rising to 15.0 billion crowns in 1998 from 12.0 billion crowns this year and 13.0 billion crowns next year.
Unemployment was seen falling to 7.6 percent of the workforce in 1998, from an expected 8.8 percent in 1996 and 8.0 percent in 1997.
